plants.name: Colchicum autumnale
plants.description: Pale pink-lilac, goblet-shaped flowers pop up from damp meadow grass with no leaves in sight. They look like a crocus that arrived months late, and they stand out in the fading green of early autumn.
plants.location: Meadows and woodland edges across Europe, including the UK and central Europe; also grown in gardens in temperate North America
plants.funFact: The flowers appear in autumn, but the leaves and seed capsules only emerge the following spring. This is why the plant is nicknamed 'naked ladies'. It is also the source of colchicine, a compound used in medicine, and every part of the plant is highly toxic.

plants.name: Symphyotrichum novae-angliae
plants.description: Tall, sturdy clumps are covered in daisy-like flowers with golden-yellow centers and rays in vivid purple, magenta or pink. Prairies, meadows and roadsides glow with these flowers, and butterflies and bees crowd onto them for late-season nectar.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer to autumn (August to October)
plants.location: Eastern and central North America, from prairies and wet meadows to native-plant gardens
plants.funFact: New England aster is a lifeline for migrating monarch butterflies. They refuel on its nectar as they head south in autumn. Its flower heads also close up on dull, cloudy days and open again in sunshine.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: The largest bloom in the protea family is a bowl of silky, pointed pink bracts around a crown of fuzzy, creamy center florets. It stands out on the fynbos hillsides, where it flowers through the southern hemisphere's late winter and spring.
plants.bloomingSeason: Winter to spring (roughly June to October, including mid-September)
plants.location: Fynbos of the Western and Eastern Cape, South Africa, including Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden
plants.funFact: King protea is South Africa's national flower. It belongs to a very old plant family that dates back to the age of Gondwana, and it is adapted to fire-prone fynbos, where its thick underground stems let it resprout after burns.
